current_episode.title: Thrive Causemetics: Karissa Bodnar. How a Beauty Business Made Millions for a Mission

guest.bio_context: Karissa Bodnar grew up on a small farm in Stanwood, Washington, north of Seattle, where she began formulating cosmetics in her parents' kitchen at age 10. She worked as a makeup artist at Sephora while studying marketing communications at the University of Washington, and was later hired by L'Oreal for product development after Clarisonic was acquired by the company. In 2013, after her close friend Christy Lamond died of cancer at age 24, Bodnar left L'Oreal to create Thrive Causemetics, a beauty brand built on a mission to give back to people in need.

pending_qa.q: How did a friend's death from cancer inspire a shift toward purpose-driven entrepreneurship?
pending_qa.r: In 2013, Christy Lamond, a college friend who dedicated her life to philanthropy and taught English to young girls in Tanzania and Chile, died of cancer at age 24. While Karissa was in Paris presenting to the CEO of L'Oreal at their annual Mondial conference, Christy called to say she had cancer, and she passed away nine months later. Christy's blog 'Wake Up and Live' discussed dying successfully, which profoundly influenced Karissa's decision to leave L'Oreal and create a brand with purpose.

pending_qa.q: What specific problem in the beauty industry for cancer patients inspired the creation of Thrive Causemetics?
pending_qa.r: While volunteering as a makeup artist with Look Good, Feel Better, an organization providing makeup classes to women going through cancer, Karissa discovered that women who had lost their natural lashes had no solution. Traditional mascara wouldn't work without lashes, and fake lashes with toxic glues filled with latex, parabens, and sulfates were irritating to immune-compromised people and wouldn't stay on. She wanted to create a non-toxic solution that would help people like Christy maintain their dignity and sense of self.

pending_qa.q: How did the Tom's Shoes business model influence the founding approach of Thrive Cosmetics?
pending_qa.r: Karissa woke up in the middle of the night in Los Angeles during an L'Oreal trip in 2013 and thought about how Tom's had built an engine for giving back through its shoe company. She realized the beauty industry had the budget to give back in a more meaningful way, and she decided to apply that one-for-one model to create Thrive Causemetics as a purpose-driven beauty brand.

pending_qa.q: What financial commitment and employment strategy did Karissa use to launch Thrive Causemetics?
pending_qa.r: Karissa invested approximately $100,000 of her life savings into starting Thrive Cosmetics. She also worked a full-time job in a different category—the nutrition and coffee industry at Bulletproof Coffee Company—to ensure she remained gainfully employed, as her father had always stressed the importance of maintaining employment while building the business.

pending_qa.q: What early sales challenges did Thrive Causemetics face in its first years?
pending_qa.r: Karissa struggled to get products into retail stores and pitched to major retailers including Sephora, Nordstrom, Ulta, Anthropologie, and QVC, but they did not see the vision. Sales were mainly online and tiny—a good day was $100 in revenue, and there were many days with no sales. She wiped out her entire life savings funding production through her full-time job.
